vignette:
The Weight of Altitude

Marcus is a 63-year-old Māori man who has spent the last two decades guiding wide-body aircraft across the Pacific, a career he describes as the one thing that kept him tethered to the world after he came home from service. Before he became a pilot, he was a young soldier deployed to a peacekeeping operation in the early 1980s, and what he witnessed there — the ambush that killed three men in his unit, the hours he spent pinned behind cover with a dying friend bleeding out beside him, unable to do anything but press his hands against a wound that would not stop — changed the architecture of his inner life in ways he is only beginning to name at sixty-three.

For years Marcus managed by moving. He flew long-haul routes, Sydney to Los Angeles, Auckland to London, and the cockpit became a kind of sanctuary. Up there, he tells his therapist, nothing could reach him. The routine of checklists, the hum of engines, the clean geometry of instruments — these things asked nothing of him emotionally, and he gave them everything he had. His wife, Hinerangi, raised their three children largely alone during those years, and she did so without complaint, though Marcus can see now, with some shame, how much she absorbed in his absence.

The trouble began in earnest about eighteen months ago, when a severe turbulence event over the Tasman Sea sent a flight attendant to the floor with a broken wrist and left several passengers screaming. The aircraft was never in real danger, but something in that moment — the sudden loss of control, the sounds of panic in the cabin — cracked something open in Marcus that he had spent forty years sealing shut. That night in his hotel room in Melbourne, he dreamed of the ambush for the first time in over a decade, and he woke soaked through, certain he could smell blood.

Since then, sleep has become hostile territory. He lies beside Hinerangi and watches the ceiling, his body rigid with a vigilance that has no object in the quiet suburban bedroom they share in Christchurch. When he does sleep, the dreams come — not always the ambush directly, but variations of it, a kind of theatre of helplessness in which he is always too late, always watching someone die just beyond the reach of his hands. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning and sits in the kitchen until dawn, drinking tea he doesn't taste.

At work, he has become hypervigilant in ways that concern him. He cross-checks instruments that don't need checking. He briefs his first officers with an intensity they visibly find unsettling. Any unexpected sound in the aircraft — a mechanical clunk, a change in engine tone — sends a cold wave through his chest that takes several minutes to subside. He has not told his employer any of this. The thought of losing his medical certificate feels, to Marcus, like the last door closing.

He is emotionally constricted in ways that hurt him and confuse Hinerangi. He cannot watch the news. He avoids his son, who works as a paramedic, because something about the uniform — the readiness for emergency — makes Marcus's chest tighten in a way he cannot explain without sounding, as he puts it, like a madman. He has stopped attending the community gatherings that were once important to him, the hui where he would see extended whānau, because he cannot sit in a crowd without scanning every exit.

What brings him to therapy, finally, is Hinerangi. She sat across from him at the kitchen table one morning after finding him there at four a.m. for the third time that week, and she said, quietly, that she was frightened — not of him, but for him. Marcus describes this moment with his eyes fixed on the middle distance, his jaw working. He says he has been carrying a dead man's weight for forty years, and he thinks it might be time to put it down.
